exploitation.x: The difference is that obtaining increased financial input during the production phase of the film reduces the risk during the exploitation phase.

exploration.e: From Middle French exploration, from Latin exploratio. Morphologically explore + -ation.
exploration.x: By this time, largely inspired by The Railway Magazine, I had begun to spread my wings, and had started on a long career of railway exploration.

explore.x: The boys explored all around till cold and hunger drove them back to the campfire one by one.

explosive.x: Notes: A rule set that (very probably) results in explosive growth; certainly in area if not population.

exponent.e: From Latin expōnēns, present participle of expōnō (“to expose; to exhibit, display, set out; to explain”), from ex- (“out, away”) + pōnō (“to lay, place, put”).
exponent.x: Like attracts like," explained Mrs. Mailey, who was quite as capable an exponent as her husband.

exponential.x: There's been an exponential rise in the number of crimes reported this year, compared to last year.

exporter.x: India is the leading exporter of guar gum, making up nearly 85 per cent of the global production.

expose.e: From Middle English exposen, from Old French exposer (“to lay open, set forth”), from Latin expōnō (“set forth”), with contamination from poser (“to lay, place”).
expose.x: Residents were exposed to dangerous levels of radiation.

exposition.e: From Middle English exposicioun, from Old French esposicion, from Latin expositiō, from expōnere (“to put forth”).
exposition.x: This essay has too much exposition in it.

exposure.x: Limit your exposure to harsh chemicals.

expound.e: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone and expose.
expound.x: Today I'll expound at length the theory propounded last week.

expressionism.e: Borrowed from French expressionnisme, equivalent to expression + -ism.

expressive.x: A programming language that is Turing complete is more expressive than one that is not.

expressly.x: We were expressly permitted to use the building. See – here is the note from the manager clearly stating that we have permission to use the building.

expulsion.e: From Middle English expulsioun, from Old French expulsion, from Latin expulsio, expulsionem.
expulsion.x: The scandal involved every member of the high school's football team, resulting in a flurry of expulsions, starting with the quarterback.

extant.e: First attested in 1545, from Latin extantem, extāns, present participle of extō (“to stand out, exist, be extant”), from ex- (“out”) + stō (“stand”).
extant.x: There are many narrow-gauge systems still extant.

extemporaneous.e: From Late Latin extemporāneus, from Latin ex tempore (“impromptu”).
extemporaneous.x: “Who the devil is there in Ramilly County,” muttered Amory aloud, “who would deliver Verlaine in an extemporaneous tune to a soaking haystack?”

extend.e: From Middle English extenden, from Anglo-Norman extendre, estendre, from Latin extendō (“to stretch out”).
extend.x: The desert extended for miles in all directions.

extension.e: From Middle English extensioun, from Old French estension, from Latin extensiō, extensiōnem.
extension.x: Next month the house is undergoing an extension.

extensive.x: I have done extensive research on the subject.

extensively.x: He has read and traveled extensively.

extent.e: From Middle English extente, from Anglo-Norman extente and Old French estente (“valuation of land, stretch of land”), from estendre, extendre (“extend”) (or from Latin…
extent.x: I'm a thoroughgoing pragmatist to the fullest extent of the word.

exterminate.e: Borrowed from Latin exterminātus, perfect passive participle of exterminō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“thoroughly”) + terminō (“to finish, close, end”)…
exterminate.x: We'll use poison to exterminate the rats.

external.e: From Late Middle English, from Medieval Latin externus (“outward, external”), from exter/exterus (“on the outside, outward”).
external.x: This building has some external pipework.

extinct.e: From Late Middle English extinct (“eliminated, eradicated, extinguished”), from Latin extīnctus, exstīnctus (“extinguished, quenched; destroyed, killed.
extinct.x: My breath is corrupt, my dayes are extinct, the graues are ready for me.

extinction.e: From late Middle English, borrowed from Latin extinctio (“extinction, annihilation”), from extinguere, past participle extinctus (“to extinguish”); see extinguish.
extinction.x: The extinction of a species once so numerous seemed incredible.

extinguish.e: Borrowed from Latin extinguo (“to put out (what is burning), quench, extinguish, deprive of life, destroy, abolish”), from ex (“out”) + stinguere (“to put out, quench…
extinguish.x: The rays of the sun were extinguished by the thunder clouds.

extol.e: Borrowed from Latin extollō (“elevate, raise high”).
extol.x: Extol thee—could I—then I will / By saying nothing new, / But just the tritest truth / That thou art heavenly.

extortion.x: Heck, what's a little extortion among friends?

extract.e: Borrowed from Latin extractum, neuter perfect passive participle of extrahō, from ex- (“out of”) + trahō (“to drag”).
extract.x: I used an extract of Hemingway's book to demonstrate culture shock.

extraction.e: From Old French estraction, from Medieval Latin extractio.

extradite.x: Balfour, who had sought refuge in Argentina, was extradited, and sentenced to a long term of penal servitude at Parkhurst Prison in the Isle of Wight.

extraneous.e: From Latin extrāneus (“from without, strange”). Doublet of strange. Cognate with estrange (verb), Spanish extraño.
extraneous.x: Extraneous substances were found on my cup of water.

extraterrestrial.x: Smith returns in Men In Black 3 as a veteran agent of a secret organization dedicated to policing the earth’s many extraterrestrials.

extravagance.e: Borrowed from French extravagance, from Medieval Latin extra + vagor (“to wander”).
extravagance.x: That luxury car is an extravagance you can't afford.

extravagant.e: Inherited from Middle English extravagaunt, from Middle French extravagant and its etymon Medieval Latin extravagans, present participle of extravagor (“to wander…
extravagant.x: The extravagant and erring spirit hies / To his confine.

extremism.x: For a student of American history and a foreigner like myself, it is easier to understand all these extremisms of conscience.

extricate.x: I finally managed to extricate myself from the tight jacket.

extroverted.e: A variant spelling of extraverted. Popularized as a psychological term by Phyllis Blanchard's use of extrovert in her 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte", from…
extroverted.x: The external and combustible Sulphur... is... protruded and extroverted.

exuberant.e: From Middle French exubérant, from Latin exūberāns, the present active participle of exūberō (“be abundant”).
exuberant.x: He was a man of exuberant fancy, and, withal of an authority so irresistible that, at his will, he turned his varied fancies into facts.

exult.e: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).
exult.x: I took a deep breath; a locomotive howled across-the darkness, Mobile-bound. So were we. I took off my shirt and exulted.

exultation.e: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.
exultation.x: You will experience the fun of life — the magic, the celebration, the exhilaration, and the exultation of your own spirit.

eyeball.e: From eye + ball. Compare Middle English balle off the eye, balle of þe eyȝe (“eyeball”, literally “ball of the eye”).
eyeball.x: Give this report an eyeball, will you please?

eyebrow.e: From Middle English eȝebreu, alteration of Old English ēaganbrū (“eyebrow”), equivalent to eye + brow. The corresponding Old English ēagbrǣw meant "eyelid".

eyelid.e: From Middle English eyelidd, eye-led, eiȝelid, eghe-lydd, yȝe-lydd, ehlid, yhelidd, from an unrecorded Old English *ēaghlid (“eyelid”), from Proto-West Germanic *augahlid…

eyesore.e: From Middle English eye sor, eie-sor, eyen soore, eæge-sare, equivalent to eye + sore.

eyrie.e: From Middle English eire, aire, from Old French aire or Medieval Latin aeria.
